scenes.visual: Title: Cancer as a Genetic Disease. Show a cell lineage with acquired DNA changes.

scenes.tts: Cancer is a genetic disease. But most changes in a tumor are not inherited. They arise in body cells during life. Some changes switch on genes that drive growth. Others switch off genes that restrain it. These changes matter because cells divide more or die less, and their descendants expand.

scenes.visual: Show acquired DNA changes in a body cell, then its descendants inheriting those changes. Contrast growth activation with loss of a growth restraint. Label somatic: arises during life; daughter cells receive the altered DNA.

scenes.tts: An oncogene is an accelerator stuck on. One altered copy is usually enough. A tumor suppressor is a brake. One working copy usually holds, so both copies normally must lose function. These are useful rules, with exceptions.

scenes.visual: Compare two gene-copy panels: an activated oncogene with a normal companion copy, and a tumor suppressor with one working copy versus neither working. Label usually to preserve the qualification.

scenes.tts: A tumor is usually a clone, the descendants of one cell. More changes accumulate. A driver gives its cell a selective advantage. A passenger gives no advantage and rides along as the clone expands. Mutation supplies variants. Selection favors those that divide more or die less. A resistant subline can survive treatment and expand, so treatment can fail.

scenes.visual: Build a branching cell lineage. Mark a driver on an expanding branch and a passenger carried along. Show different sublines, then treatment reducing susceptible cells while a resistant subline survives and expands. Do not depict treatment as creating the resistance change.

scenes.tts: R B one shows how inherited risk fits this picture. A child inherits one broken copy in every cell. Yet only a few retinal cells become tumors. Why? One working copy usually still provides the brake.
scenes.narration: RB1 shows how inherited risk fits this picture. A child inherits one broken copy in every cell. Yet only a few retinal cells become tumors. Why? One working copy usually still provides the brake.
scenes.caption: RB1 shows how inherited risk fits this picture. A child inherits one broken copy in every cell. Yet only a few retinal cells become tumors. Why? One working copy usually still provides the brake.
scenes.visual: Reuse the RB1 cell grid: every cell has one broken copy and one working copy. Highlight only a few retinal cells as candidates for a later second hit. Keep the working-copy brake visible.

scenes.tts: The inherited change is the first hit. A rare second hit removes the working copy's function. Often this is loss of heterozygosity: the cell keeps only the mutant allele. Deletion, chromosome loss or mitotic recombination can supply that second hit.

scenes.visual: Reuse the second-hit grid. Zoom into one RB1 carrier cell. Show alternative routes: deletion of the working region, loss of the working chromosome, and mitotic recombination leaving two mutant copies of the region. Label loss of heterozygosity. Do not show recombination as deletion.

scenes.tts: Without a germline first hit, both hits must arise in the same body cell. These tumors tend to be single, one-sided and diagnosed later.

scenes.visual: Compare the inherited-first-hit pathway with a nonhereditary pathway starting with two working RB1 copies. The latter acquires both hits in one cell lineage. Show a single affected eye and a later diagnosis, without probability figures.

scenes.tts: So the inherited allele is dominant in a family but recessive in the cell. A pedigree tracks risk. A cell needs both copies disabled.

scenes.visual: Reuse the pedigree beside the RB1 cell. Label family: inherited risk; cell: both RB1 copies disabled. Keep this statement explicitly tied to RB1.

scenes.tts: Genome instability adds variation. Faulty D N A repair can increase mutations. Faulty chromosome segregation produces chromosome gains and losses. That variation supplies more material for selection.
scenes.narration: Genome instability adds variation. Faulty DNA repair can increase mutations. Faulty chromosome segregation produces chromosome gains and losses. That variation supplies more material for selection.
scenes.caption: Genome instability adds variation. Faulty DNA repair can increase mutations. Faulty chromosome segregation produces chromosome gains and losses. That variation supplies more material for selection.
scenes.visual: Show defective DNA repair adding sequence changes and faulty chromosome segregation producing gains and losses. Feed these alternative sources of variation into a branching tumor lineage.

scenes.tts: Sequencing a tumor and matched normal tissue helps separate somatic from germline changes. Variants in both are usually germline. Variants only in the tumor are usually somatic. The tumor sample also contains normal cells, so its purity matters when reading variant fractions.

scenes.visual: Show tumor and matched-normal samples, with shared variants labeled usually germline and tumor-only variants labeled usually somatic. Show normal cells mixed into the tumor sample and define purity as the fraction of tumor cells. End on the branching tumor lineage; omit numerical allele fractions.
End card: Cancer as a Genetic Disease, above the acquired-change cell lineage.
